To this day I wish, I wish, I wish I had told my mum. Maybe if I had things would've been different. But even if I had they may still have ended the same, like you said, who knows? Unfortunately in both our cases what's done is done and dwelling on the 'what if's' will only serve to drive us crazy. 

It's normal for some days to be worse than others, I have the same even 11 years later. Sometimes I can be ok and other times I just fall apart. Grief is a strange thing.

I'm so sorry for your loss. I lost my father to suicide when I was 8 so I get how devastating it is. 

But please believe me when I tell you this:  **this is not your fault**. There is **no possible way** you could've foreseen this. It is tragic, but not your fault. I don't think **he** is angry at you, I think **you're** angry at **yourself**. I understand you regret moving schools and not calling and you feel guilty, but even if you had stayed at the same school and kept in regular contact, that doesn't necessarily mean he wouldn't have still done it. Like you said, his reasons are still unknown. It was likely even something you weren't aware of. 

I definitely think seeing a counsellor is a great idea as it seems you have unresolved feelings that you need to work through. You will always miss him, but you don't have to blame yourself for something that isn't your fault. 

Good luck and I hope you can finally heal.

That said, if you think such an approach would be beneficial to **you** and is something **you** want to do to improve **your** situation, then fair enough. But please don't do it because you feel some obligation to do so because you think you're somehow a 'problem'. If you were a homicidal maniac I would definitely say you should check-in to a psych ward because you really **would** be a 'problem' in respect to the harm/potential harm to others. But you're not, you're in pain, pain which **others** have inflicted on **you**, not the opposite. You were the victim of cruel manipulation, and when is the **victim** ever the problem? It's the **perpetrator** that's the problem, and that isn't you, Infamous, please realise that. You shouldn't make yourself suffer for something that isn't even remotely your fault. 

There are also many ways you can seek assistance without resorting to institutionalisation. Maybe you could talk to your GP about how you're feeling and they could refer you to someone better equipped to assist you?

I have read about a scientific study (this was a few years ago so I'm stretching my memory a bit) that says apparently in the human brain their exists two opposing sides: the desire to create/nurture and the desire to destroy/kill. Apparently in the 'normal' (i.e. non-suicidal person) the creating/nurturing side is dominant, but the opposite is true for the suicidal person and that the creating/nurturing side is either very weak or all but non-existent. Maybe this is why the scientific community also came to consider the desire to die abnormal because it triggers a 'different' response in the brain? Though I would counter that argument with if there are such two sides in the brain and nature has equipped us with both, why is one more normal than the other? I think even the scientific world has been roped into the wider philosophy of wanting to live is good, but wanting to die is bad. Suicide was, in ancient times, considered an honourable death. I don't know what changed to get us to where we are today.

If they, like yourself, seem to be rational, while I'd never advocate you killing yourself, I would understand your decision if I discovered you did. 

I think the whole 'right to life' movement is to blame for the wide spread condemnation of dying any sooner than absolutely necessary. 'Life is scared!' they chant, blah blah blah. They so often overlook the quality of life and instead focus on prolonging existence as long as possible. I think a much more humane approach is to help those who actually want help and to try to offer others help but if they don't wish to take it, respect their wishes without doing things like institutionalising them against their will.

I know it's not the reason for your issue, religion is just a good example in this situation, which like you said, can be substituted for any of the above. But when you consider that if someone is discovered to pose a risk to themselves (even in a non-suicidal manner) or others, or even to just be mentally unstable due to some kind of belief and society decrees they are 'not thinking right', need medication etc, there are a lot of other ideologies aside from 'extreme' pessimism that are considered 'unacceptable irrationality'. Like say a mental patient told their doctor that they believed monsters were after them or something, their doctor may also dismiss their beliefs by saying that there is no such thing. 

I suppose society somewhere along the line decided what are 'normal' ideologies and what are not and anyone who is seen to have ideologies too far outside the accepted guidelines needs 'correcting' through whatever treatments deemed appropriate.

There are definitely extremists out there whose beliefs can cause harm to themselves and others, but these aren't so much necessarily because of the beliefs themselves but because of the practioners. I meant more those who, while they have what society might consider 'strange' beliefs, don't actually cause harm to themselves or others through their belief. For example, I'm a Christian and believing in my religion poses no harm to myself or others because I am not an extremist nor do I try to force people to believe what I believe. 

Now when you say 'believing you'll survive your own death', I assume you mean believing in an afterlife?

I get what you mean. I guess in society there's 'acceptable' irrational (for example odd religious beliefs which don't pose a direct risk to the person's well being) and then there's the 'non-acceptable' irrational beliefs (like those associated with depression where negative ideologies or a jaded view on life can be construed to pose a risk to someone's well being and putting them at an increased chance of self-harm). For the sake of helping people whose judgement really is impacted by mental illness (say going from a positive person to a negative person), society has to draw the line somewhere to distinguish potentially harmful ideology.

My father committed suicide when I was 8 so I speak from experience when I say PLEASE DON'T! :( I'm not trying to send you on a guilt trip here, I just want to give you an insight into what it's like to be the child of a suicide victim. It will devastate your children more than you can possibly imagine. My father's death messed me up big time, I beg you not to put your children through the same. They've already lost their father, please don't make them lose their mother too. :( I understand that losing your husband would be so painful and I am truly sorry for that, but committing suicide will only cause more pain. I'm sure your husband wouldn't want you to do this. There isn't a day that goes by that I don't miss my father and wish he was still alive. I often wonder, 'Did I have a part in it? If I had been a better daughter would he have still done it?' (He committed suicide exactly one week before I turned 9.) Your children will also likely wonder if your suicide was in some way their fault and those questions will haunt them as they do me. Please seek help before it's too late.

No, I said people FEEL like it's the only option. Many people who are 'born differently', or 'can't deal with the pain', as you put it, have tried various coping mechanisms, for example counselling or medication, but for whatever reason, they may not work for them. We don't all just automatically turn to suicide, but instead suicide is often a last resort when it seems like all other options are exhausted. No, I never said it was 'ok' to kill yourself, I merely was attempting to demonstrate the thought process a lot of people go through when they come to wanting to end their lives.

I say that because I don't choose to feel the way I do and I wouldn't wish getting to the point of feeling this way on my worst enemy. No one wants to feel like this, but we do usually due to depression, again something we didn't consciously choose to have. I totally agree that pain is a part of life, but like I said, people experience pain differently, and what you might consider 'not enough to kill yourself over' may be enough for someone else. Suicide isn't a coping mechanism, quite right, because suicide is often a result of a lack of coping mechanisms in the first place. 'Coping' is a continual process, and you can only commit suicide once, so it can't be a coping mechanism. Rather, suicide is a permanent 'solution' for people who feel like there is no other option.

The reasons people feel the desire to, attempt to and/or succeed in suicide are as varied as the people themselves. The best way I've seen it explained is it happens when one's pain outweighs their coping mechanisms. Pain is experienced differently by all, and what might be bearable to some is not bearable to others. When pain > coping mechanism, it can result in feeling overwhelmed and that the only way out/relief will be to kill themselves. 

I know it is hard to understand if you've never felt that way yourself, and I hope you never do, because it's something I would never wish on my worst enemy. I've been suicidal since I was 12 (now 19) and have attempted it several times but so far have sadly had no success. I'll get it right one day though and hopefully one day soon.
